 After K-beauty, China’s cosmetics brands set sights on global market 
 Chinese cosmetics companies are expanding into the United States, Europe and Asia, hoping to replicate the international success of Korean beauty brands after overtaking foreign competitors in their home market.
 October 27, 2026 • 
 12:10 AM 
 Share
 Chinese cosmetics companies are expanding into the United States, Europe and Asia, hoping to replicate the international success of Korean beauty brands after overtaking foreign competitors in their home market.
 Proya Cosmetics, China’s largest domestic beauty brand by revenue, will begin selling two skincare lines in 400 Ulta Beauty stores across the United States in November. The products will also be available through Ulta’s website.
 The company opened a research and development center in Paris this month as part of its international expansion.
 Other Chinese brands are also establishing a presence overseas.
 Florasis, known for intricately carved lipsticks and cosmetics inspired by traditional Chinese designs, opened its first overseas flagship store in Tokyo’s Ginza shopping district last year.
 Joocyee and Judydoll, both owned by China’s Joy Group, opened stores in Singapore last year. Their products are also sold through British Asian beauty retailer Skin Cupid.
 The expansion follows a decade of rapid growth for Chinese cosmetics companies, which have taken market share from established international brands.
 Domestic brands accounted for 57.4% of China’s $159 billion cosmetics market in 2025, according to the China Association of Fragrance, Flavor and Cosmetic Industries. They overtook foreign brands in 2022.
 Proya wants to become one of the world’s 10 largest cosmetics brands and is exploring acquisitions of smaller foreign companies.
 Its majority-owned makeup brand Flower Knows, recognized for elaborate fairytale-inspired packaging, entered British retailer Boots in March and began selling in selected Ulta stores in September.
 Proya founder and CEO Hou Juncheng acknowledged that the company remains largely unknown outside China.
 “I would say that Proya’s brand awareness in both Europe and the US is currently zero,” Hou said at the opening of its Paris research center.
 “We hope that through collaboration with our partners, we can earn consumer trust and encourage them to purchase our products.”
 Chinese companies are following a path established by South Korean cosmetics makers, whose international sales have grown sharply.
 South Korea’s beauty exports increased 50% over five years to reach $11.4 billion in 2025. The country surpassed France in 2024 as the largest source of cosmetics imported into the United States, according to US International Trade Commission data.
 Chinese brands are competing with products that include skincare-infused makeup, freeze-dried face masks and creams containing ingredients used in traditional Chinese medicine.
 Their relatively affordable prices could also help attract consumers looking for alternatives to expensive skincare products, according to Elisa Harca, co-founder of marketing firm Red Ant Asia.
 But the companies face challenges in building international recognition and navigating trade tensions between China and the United States.
 Florasis president of global markets Gabby Chen said US-China tensions prompted the company to shift its international expansion away from the American market last year.
 She said the company remains focused on developing its international business regardless of political developments.
 The overseas push comes as Chinese consumer companies seek new sources of revenue following years of weak domestic spending.
 Beauty brands are joining Chinese electric vehicle makers, electronics companies, fashion retailers and beverage chains in expanding beyond their home market.
